name: PhastFT
baseline: FFTW 3.3.8 (via the Rust fftw crate); also RustFFT
workload: Single-threaded complex-to-complex forward and inverse FFT, f32 and f64, power-of-two lengths 8 to 8,388,608, divan benchmark on an M1 MacBook Pro in a third-party benchmark repo (astral4/fft-benchmark).
claimed_speedup: f32 N=1024: 4.749 us (PhastFT) vs 7.291 us (FFTW) forward; f32 N=1,048,576: 10.21 ms vs 14.20 ms; f32 N=8,388,608: 109.0 ms vs 193.3 ms (RustFFT 103.9 ms). Third-party conclusion: 'phastft was the fastest in most tests, but rustfft was the fastest on the smallest and largest sequence lengths tested' and 'fftw was consistently slower than both rustfft and phastft'. Memory: 8.388 MB (PhastFT) vs 41.94 MB (RustFFT) at f32 N=2^20 (derived from page data, about 5x less).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.80.0-nightly (2024-05-03); phastft v0.2.1, rustfft v6.2.0, fftw crate v0.8.0 over FFTW 3.3.8 compiled with Apple clang 15.0.0; cargo profile and FFTW configure flags not stated
hardware: M1 MacBook Pro (exact variant not stated). PhastFT's own README plots use a MacBook Air with Apple M2, 4P+4E cores, 24 GB, multi-threaded.
tradeoffs: Power-of-two lengths only. Runtime SIMD selection (no -C target-cpu=native needed). In-place algorithm with much lower memory than RustFFT. Optional multi-threading through the 'parallel' feature. The 2024 benchmark used v0.2.1, which needed nightly Rust for portable SIMD; the current Cargo.toml says rust-version 1.88.
caveats: Independent but small personal benchmark repo from 2024 (not a well-known suite), Apple Silicon only, cargo flags not stated, single machine. The FFTW times look high for small N (about 1.4 us at N=8), which suggests the FFTW 3.3.8 build or the binding did not use NEON codelets or adds per-call overhead; treat the FFTW comparison on Apple Silicon with caution. RustFFT beats PhastFT at N<=32 and N>=2^22 (f32). PhastFT's own README benchmarks (M2, multi-threaded, vs RustFFT and FFTW3) are plots only, with no numbers in text.
found_via: GitHub topic page fft (Rust) and the benches/README of QuState/PhastFT; numbers from astral4/fft-benchmark README

name: RustFFT
workload: Single-threaded complex-to-complex forward and inverse FFT, f32 and f64, power-of-two lengths 8 to 8,388,608, in the third-party astral4/fft-benchmark (divan) on an M1 MacBook Pro.
claimed_speedup: f32 N=8,388,608: 103.9 ms (RustFFT) vs 193.3 ms (FFTW); f32 N=16: 124.6 ns vs 1.405 us; f32 N=1,048,576: 12.49 ms vs 14.20 ms; f64 N=65,536: 754.4 us vs 953.5 us. Slower than FFTW for f32 forward at N=1024 to 16384 (e.g. N=4096: 45.33 us vs 21.20 us). Third-party conclusion: 'fftw was consistently slower than both rustfft and phastft'.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.80.0-nightly (2024-05-03); rustfft v6.2.0, fftw crate v0.8.0 over FFTW 3.3.8 compiled with Apple clang 15.0.0; cargo profile and FFTW configure flags not stated
hardware: M1 MacBook Pro (exact variant not stated)
stars_or_usage: 942 stars; most widely used pure-Rust FFT crate
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, any length including primes in O(n log n), SIMD for x86-64 (AVX, SSE), AArch64 (NEON) and WebAssembly. No built-in multithreading. Needs a recent Rust toolchain (README says 1.86+).
caveats: Third-party, single machine, Apple Silicon only, sizes are powers of two only. The FFTW numbers at small N look inflated (about 1.4 us at N=8), so the FFTW build may not have used NEON codelets. RustFFT is slower than the FFTW column in the mid range (N=1024 to 16384 f32). The ejmahler/RustFFT page itself states no numbers against FFTW; a Rust-forum post titled 'RustFFT 5.0.0 experimental 1 now faster than FFTW' appeared in search results but could not be opened from this container.
found_via: GitHub: README of astral4/fft-benchmark (surfaced by a search for PhastFT benchmarks); repo page of ejmahler/RustFFT

name: gpu_fftw
baseline: FFTW3 (running on the Raspberry Pi CPU)
workload: Binary-compatible FFTW3 replacement that offloads power-of-two complex FFTs (log2 N from 8 to 21, float) to the Raspberry Pi GPU (Andrew Holme's GPU_FFT); the README self-test compares ffts per second against CPU fftw3.
claimed_speedup: Self-test output: 'GPU FFTW 7.11652 times faster (11523.3 ffts/sec, 86.781 usec/fft, fftw3: 1619.23 ffts/sec)'. README: 'They can be up to ten times faster than running fftw3 by itself.'
compiler_and_flags: Makefile cross-compiles with RPICC/RPICXX using -march=armv6 -mfloat-abi=hard -mfpu=vfp -O3 -ffast-math (-std=c99, -std=c++11); the README example run does not state the flags used
hardware: Raspberry Pi (model not stated in the README; the Makefile targets armv6, i.e. original Pi class)
tradeoffs: Float only (double only through lossy 'double squashing'), power-of-two sizes 2^8 to 2^21, 1-D complex only (no 2-D/3-D/real), copies arrays to GPU memory, needs root, falls back to FFTW3 otherwise. Early alpha by the author's own words.
caveats: First-party numbers from one sample self-test output; FFT size, Pi model and CPU clock not stated in the README. Single Raspberry Pi generation from 2015 (pre-Pi 4); the GPU_FFT code it relies on belongs to a different author and its license was not checked. Repo is abandoned since January 2015.
found_via: WebSearch 'FFT library faster than FFTW benchmark github' result page for gpu-fftw/gpu_fftw

name: go-fft
baseline: FFTW 3.3.11 (native C, FFTW_MEASURE plans, NEON); also scipy.fft/numpy.fft (pocketfft) and gonum
workload: Pure-Go (CGO=0) complex128 and float64 FFTs on one Apple M4 Max: 1-D complex, real (r2c, c2r) and 2-D complex, compared against native FFTW run through a C harness, numpy/scipy and gonum, single-threaded for 1-D, multicore fan-out for go-fft 2-D.
claimed_speedup: Only the large 2-D rows beat FFTW: 1024x1024 2.78 ms vs 6.30 ms, 512x512 0.634 ms vs 1.247 ms, 256x256 0.208 ms vs 0.271 ms (go-fft multicore vs single-threaded FFTW). 1-D complex 256 points: 716 ns (go-fft) vs 419 ns (FFTW) vs 2,302 ns (scipy.fft), so it beats scipy.fft/pocketfft about 3.2x but lags FFTW 1.2x to 3.3x on 1-D complex. Report: 'vs FFTW (native C, gold standard): 3/24 ops at-or-above parity (the three large 2-D multicore shapes)'; vs gonum 19/19 ops faster.
compiler_and_flags: go1.26.4 darwin/arm64, -benchtime=1s; FFTW 3.3.11 Homebrew arm64 bottle (NEON) called from C; numpy 2.5.0, scipy 1.18.0, gonum v0.16.0; no Go build flags stated
tradeoffs: Pure Go with no cgo, any length (Rader's algorithm for 7-smooth N-1 primes, Bluestein chirp-z otherwise, per its README), complex and real transforms, 2-D. SIMD butterflies routed to SSE2/AVX2 on amd64 and compiler-autovectorized NEON on arm64.
caveats: Mostly loses to FFTW: 1-D rows lag FFTW by 1.2x to 3.3x. The only wins are 2-D 256x256 and larger, where go-fft uses all cores and FFTW is pinned to one thread, so the 2-D comparison is not like-for-like. BENCHMARKS.md itself says the complex, real and 2-D tables were not regenerated after later changes and that the host was under background load. Very new project (1 star). The clearer win is against gonum (3x to 5x on composite sizes, an order of magnitude on primes) and against scipy.fft/numpy at small N.
found_via: WebSearch 'Go OR Zig OR Nim OR Julia pure FFT library benchmark faster than FFTW github' result page for go-fft/fft; BENCHMARKS.md opened for numbers

name: FINUFFT
baseline: NFFT3 (Chemnitz NFFT library, which uses FFTW); also CMCL NUFFT
workload: Non-uniform FFT (type 1, 2D, M=500,000 nonuniform points, 300x200 output modes, single thread, relative error about 1e-13) in the repo's NFFT3 migration tutorial.
claimed_speedup: Tutorial run: NFFT3 0.589 s vs FINUFFT 0.0787 s, 'a 7.5x speed-up (Both use a single thread, tested on the same AMD 5700U laptop)'. docs/related.rst: NFFT 'significantly slower and/or more memory-intensive than FINUFFT'; CMCL NUFFT 'Much (up to 50x even for one thread) slower than FINUFFT'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the tutorial (CI performance page uses cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release)
stars_or_usage: 445 stars; used by many NUFFT users (docs/users.rst lists them)
tradeoffs: Nonuniform FFT only (types 1, 2, 3 in 1-3 dimensions), CPU and GPU (cuFINUFFT); relies on FFTW or DUCC for its internal uniform FFT. NFFT3 offers more transform types (inverse, sphere, rotation group).
caveats: Not a replacement for an ordinary FFT; the baseline is a NUFFT library, not FFTW, and is not in the category baseline list. The 7.5x figure is a single tutorial run, not a systematic benchmark. The README cites a peer-reviewed paper (SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 41(5), C479-C504, 2019) with the multi-library comparison, but that paper could not be opened here, so the tier may be raisable to B. docs/related.rst also says DUCC's NUFFT is faster in some regimes, and NFFT.jl beat FINUFFT v2.2.0 by up to 1.7x in multithreaded type 1/2 (author statement in docs/users.rst).
found_via: WebSearch 'FINUFFT benchmark faster than NFFT github flatironinstitute nonuniform FFT library'; docs/related.rst and docs/nfft_migr.rst

name: JTransforms
baseline: FFTW 3 through the ezFFTW Java wrapper (single-threaded)
workload: Java JMH benchmark: full real-to-complex forward FFT, zero the DC bin, then inverse FFT, for 1-D (1,024 to 10,000,000 elements) and 2-D (1280x720 to 5000x5000) arrays, in the third-party FFTBench repo.
claimed_speedup: Pure-Java JTransforms vs FFTW wrapper: 1-D 10,000,000 elements 3.205 s vs 4.560 s; 1-D 1,024 elements about 1e-4 s vs 0.006 s; 2-D 1280x720 single array 0.058 s multithreaded and 0.137 s single-threaded vs 0.155 s; 2-D 1920x1080 0.125 s / 0.331 s vs 0.360 s. FFTW is faster at 1-D 98,304 to 1,000,000 (e.g. 1,000,000: 0.175 s vs 0.290 s) and at 2-D 1087x1931 single-threaded (0.998 s vs 2.132 s).
compiler_and_flags: Java with JMH; Java version and JVM flags not stated
tradeoffs: Pure Java, multithreaded by default, DFT/DCT/DST/DHT derived from Ooura's FFT package; JVM warm-up and GC apply.
caveats: Mixed result: the benchmark author's own conclusion is that no library wins everywhere. FFTW is reached through a Java wrapper (ezFFTW, written by the benchmark's author), so JNI and copying overhead may favor JTransforms. CPU, Java version and flags are not stated, and each JMH row used only 3 iterations. The JTransforms README itself shows no FFTW numbers.
found_via: WebSearch 'JTransforms github Java FFT benchmark compared to FFTW multithreaded speed' result page for hageldave/FFTBench

name: AppleSiliconFFT
workload: Batched single-precision complex FFT on the Apple M1 GPU (Metal kernels), N=4096, batch=256, GFLOPS vs vDSP on the same machine.
claimed_speedup: Radix-8 Stockham kernel 138.45 GFLOPS (1.78 us per FFT) vs vDSP 107.0 GFLOPS (2.29 us per FFT), '+29%'; in-place CT with simdgroup_matrix 128 GFLOPS (+20%); radix-4 Stockham 113.6 GFLOPS (+6%). Multi-size (batch=64): 53 GFLOPS at N=256 to 138 at N=4096, 84-103 at N=8192-16384. README for M6: SME2 radix-8 CPU FFT 'beats vDSP by up to 5.3x'; N=8192/16384 one-pass GPU kernels '2.2x / 1.85x faster than MPSGraph'.
compiler_and_flags: xcrun metal and metallib, swiftc -O -framework Metal -framework Accelerate; macOS 13+
tradeoffs: GPU-only Metal kernels, power-of-two sizes 256 to 16384 (four-step for larger), single precision; N=4096 batch workload; Apple Silicon only.
caveats: Compares a GPU kernel with the CPU vDSP library, batch=256 throughput, with data resident on the GPU, so it is not an end-to-end comparison including host transfers. The paper is a preprint only (no peer review). vDSP is not in the category baseline list. Tier A is on reproducibility (public harness, flags, M1) and could be lowered if the verifier cannot run it.
found_via: WebSearch 'Radix-8 Stockham FFT Apple Silicon Metal beating vDSP github repository'

name: Auto-MPFT
baseline: FFTW and Intel MKL (full FFT, then keep the needed coefficients); also Pruned FFT and PFT
workload: Computing only a small subset of Fourier coefficients of multidimensional arrays (synthetic 2^n x 2^n for n=8..15 and real image sets such as Cityscapes, ADE20K, DF2K, RiceLeaf, Bird).
claimed_speedup: 'Auto-MPFT surpasses existing partial Fourier transform methods and optimized FFT libraries, achieving up to 7.6x increase in speed without sacrificing accuracy' (KDD 2024 abstract in the README).
tradeoffs: Approximates only a chosen subset of coefficients (partial Fourier transform) and so wins only when the output is much smaller than the input; needs MKL, IPP and FFTW installed to build the comparison code. Hyperparameters chosen automatically by a convex solver.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (KDD 2024, per the README) but the README has no result table, hardware or compiler flags, and the 7.6x figure is a maximum over all datasets and baselines. Does not produce the full FFT output. The predecessor PFT (snudatalab/PFT, KDD 2021, C++, Apache-2.0, 16 stars) makes the same kind of claim against FFTW and MKL but its README states no numbers.
found_via: WebSearch 'Fast Partial Fourier Transform PFT github code faster than FFTW MKL' result page for snudatalab/Auto-MPFT

name: MPSFT (Matrix Pencil Sparse Fourier Transform)
workload: Sparse Fourier transform of an N=2^22 signal with S nonzero frequencies, single core, Google Benchmark, FFTW built from source on the same machine.
claimed_speedup: 'For N=2^22, we are faster than FFTW when S is less than around 1800.' README timings: MPSFT at N=4,194,301 S=64 19.38 ms, S=1024 140.8 ms, S=4096 502.3 ms; FFTW at N=4,194,304 225.3 ms (FFTW_ESTIMATE) and 102.3 ms (FFTW_MEASURE). So S=64 is about 5.3x faster than FFTW_MEASURE (derived from page data) while the README itself notes 'the sparsity has to be around 1000 in order for MPSFT to be faster than FFTW'.
compiler_and_flags: Bazel --config=opt, FFTW built from source (--enable-shared --enable-threads --enable-openmp), Google Benchmark release mode; compiler version not stated
hardware: Not stated (CPU frequency scaling disabled, single core)
tradeoffs: Only useful for signals that are exactly or nearly sparse in frequency; approximate output; depends on FFTW, Eigen and Boost.SIMD.
caveats: Abandoned since 2017. README says 'For now, we will use the GPL license' because of FFTW, but the repo has no LICENSE file, so treat as reference. Hardware and compiler not stated; benchmark sizes differ slightly (N=4,194,301 vs 4,194,304). The win applies only to sparse inputs (S below roughly 1000-1800 of 4 million bins) and README says SFFT1/SFFT2 (other sparse algorithms) are faster at larger S.
found_via: WebSearch 'sparse FFT sFFT github code faster than FFTW sparse Fourier transform implementation' result page for jiaweichiu/mpsft

name: FlashFFTConv
baseline: PyTorch FFT convolution (torch.fft, backed by cuFFT)
workload: Gated long convolution via FFT on one H100-SXM, batch 64, hidden dimension 768, sequence lengths 256 to 4M, bf16/fp16.
claimed_speedup: README table: 5.64x at 256, 7.93x at 1K, 6.64x at 4K, 5.42x at 8K, 2.45x at 16K, 3.22x at 32K, 1.74x at 1M, 1.37x at 2M, 1.30x at 4M (e.g. 1K: 0.29 ms vs 2.30 ms); up to 8.21x less memory; 'up to 7.93 times faster than PyTorch FFT convolutions'.
compiler_and_flags: Nvidia PyTorch docker container 23.05, PyTorch 2.0, CUDA; nvcc flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 355 stars; README says it targets language models such as Monarch Mixer, H3 and Hyena
tradeoffs: FP16 and BF16 only, power-of-two FFT sizes 256 to 4,194,304, Ampere/Hopper GPUs, fused Monarch-decomposition kernels that use tensor cores; computes convolutions, not a general FFT API.
caveats: The baseline is PyTorch's FFT convolution, not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT, and is a GPU task, so it only speaks to the cuFFT/PyTorch route. Gain shrinks to 1.3x at 4M tokens. The README cites an ICLR 2024 paper (peer review is stated only in the BibTeX; the paper page could not be opened here). Benchmark script is benchmarks/benchmark_flashfftconv.py.
found_via: WebSearch 'FlashFFTConv github HazyResearch flash-fft-conv speedup over cuFFT PyTorch FFT convolution'

name: minfft
baseline: KissFFT (also PocketFFT; FFTW SSE2 shown as reference)
workload: Speed (Mflops) of one-dimensional double-precision in-place forward complex DFT of size N=2^1 to 2^20, plotted in docs/speed.svg.
claimed_speedup: README states only plots of speed and accuracy 'compared with the libraries of similar design: KissFFT and PocketFFT', with FFTW shown for reference. Values read from the plot data (derived from page data, approximate): minfft about 2.2k to 10.8k Mflops vs KissFFT about 0.8k to 5.2k Mflops, i.e. roughly 1.35x to 4.5x KissFFT at every size N=2^1 to 2^20 (for example 6,525 vs 1,870 Mflops at N=4 and 1,948 vs 1,058 at N=2^20). Against PocketFFT minfft is faster for N up to about 2^6 (6,525 vs 1,762 Mflops at N=4) and at N=2^17 to 2^18, but about 5% to 25% slower for N=2^7 to 2^16 and at N=2^19 to 2^20 (for example 7,270 vs 9,094 at N=2^11 and 1,948 vs 2,554 at N=2^20). The FFTW SSE2 reference is about 1.1x to 2.7x faster than minfft.
tradeoffs: Power-of-two lengths only, tiny C89 (and Fortran 2003) code base, FFTW-style interface option; complex, real, cosine and sine transforms in any dimension.
caveats: No text numbers: the figures are read from the SVG plot geometry (calibrated against the axis ticks) and are approximate. Hardware, compiler and flags are not stated, and the benchmark code is not in the README. Slower than PocketFFT over much of the mid and large range and than the FFTW SSE2 reference everywhere.
found_via: GitHub topic page cooley-tukey (aimukhin/minfft 'A small and fast Discrete Fourier Transform library'); README and docs/speed.svg

name: Ne10 (NEON FFT)
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec FFT (assembly); also tricl_fft and CkFft
workload: Complex FFT of length 1024 on an Android Samsung Galaxy S6, cycles per FFT, measured by an author of a competing FFT library (SuperpoweredFFT) in a GitHub issue.
claimed_speedup: Cycles per 1024-point complex FFT: SuperpoweredFFT 7,375; ne10_fft 10,125; libavcodec 14,375; tricl_fft_fft 21,833; CkFft 25,000. So Ne10 is about 1.4x faster than libavcodec (derived from page data) but 37% slower than SuperpoweredFFT.
tradeoffs: Arm NEON-optimized FFT (assembly noted for the FFT in the issue comment) for ARMv7 and AArch64 with a complex FFT sample in the repo; part of a larger NEON math library.
caveats: Weak evidence: a single issue comment with one size, one phone and no methodology or Ne10 version. It does not compare to KissFFT or FFTW. Ne10's own ARM blog post claims it is faster than FFTW, KissFFT and pffft on ARM, but that page could not be opened here, so those numbers are not recorded. Last commit 2018.
found_via: WebSearch 'Ne10 FFT NEON faster than KissFFT github projectNe10' result page for the Ne10 issue tracker
